text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Commercial bank Nordbanken's ongoing share buy-back scheme is turning into a scandal. Many private investors have been tempted to sell their holdings at a price way below their current market value.

- Sweden would not need to change a consitutional clause giving the Riksbank (central bank) a monopoly on issuing banknotes if the country were to become a member of the currency union of the EMU. The Riksbank would retain its monopoly but as a subordinate body to the European central bank, a professor of European law says.
- Deputy Riksbank Governor Lars Heikensten says there is room for more cuts in the central bank's key repo rate.
- Around 200,000 jobs disappeared in Swedish industry between 1990 and 1995. Staff cuts have totalled 11,000 at 19 major workplaces over the period.
- Uncertainty surrounding a reform of the pension system will be discussed by party leaders. Prime Minister Goran Persson has mooted the idea and will probably call a meeting later this autumn.
- Truck makers Volvo and Mack have settled out of court after Mack accused the Swedish group of illegally poaching U.S. Volvo Truck's new president Marc Gustafsson.

- Swedish forestry products and steel are not selling well in Germany. The two product groups, which account for around two-fifths of Sweden's exports to Germany, lost around 20 percent of their market value over the first half of the year.
- Banks find it difficult to take women entrepreneurs seriously, a new study shows. Women seeking business loans are often met with scepticism by male bank employees.

- Jan Carendi, vice president of insurer Skandia, and group CEO Lars-Eric Peterson are on a collision course over the fate of Skandia's overseas unit AFS. Carendi wants to spin off AFS, whilst Petersson aims to keep the unit the group.
